Following clusters over time

Source: vignettes/articles/following-clusters-over-time.qmd

The previous guides built one network and found its clusters. A single network of a long period, however, puts side by side literatures that never coexisted, and hides how a literature is born, grows, splits or fades. This guide follows the dynamic workflow that is the core of networkflow: one network per time window, clusters in each window, and a rule that links the clusters of successive windows into dynamic clusters whose history can be told and drawn.

One network per window

We build bibliographic coupling networks of the explanations of the stagflation on sliding ten-year windows (1975-1984, 1976-1985…, 2004-2013), keep the main component of each, and detect clusters in each window with Leiden.

library(networkflow)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidygraph)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")
networks <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 10,
  window_step = 1,
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1,
  filter_components = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
networks <- add_clusters(
  networks,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  seed = 123,
  verbose = FALSE
)
n_window_clusters <- sum(sapply(networks, function(graph) {
  length(unique(as_tibble(graph, active = "nodes")$cluster_leiden))
}))
c(windows = length(networks), clusters = n_window_clusters)
 windows clusters
      30      110

Each window has its own clusters, numbered “01”, “02”… These numbers mean nothing across windows: cluster “01” of 1975-1984 and cluster “01” of 1976-1985 may be two different literatures.

Linking clusters across windows

The rule

merge_dynamic_clusters() links each cluster to a cluster of the previous window when they share most of their documents. Let VaV_a be the documents of cluster aa in window t−1t-1, and VbV_b those of cluster bb in window tt. Cluster bb inherits the identifier of aa when a majority of aa goes to bband a majority of bb comes from aa:

|Va∩Vb|Da>τand|Va∩Vb|Db>τ, \frac{|V_a \cap V_b|}{D_a} > \tau \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{|V_a \cap V_b|}{D_b} > \tau,

with τ\tau the threshold_similarity, strictly above 0.5 so that each cluster inherits at most one identifier and passes it to at most one cluster. The denominators depend on similarity_type:

  • "complete": Da=|Va|D_a = |V_a| and Db=|Vb|D_b = |V_b|, all the documents of both clusters;
  • "partial": only the documents present in both windows count, Da=|Va∩Vt|D_a = |V_a \cap V_t| and Db=|Vb∩Vt−1|D_b = |V_b \cap V_{t-1}|.

With sliding windows, window tt loses the documents of the first year of window t−1t-1 and gains those of a new year. With "complete", a cluster that recruits many new documents, or loses many old ones, may lose its identifier because its composition changed. With "partial", only the documents present in both windows are compared, and a cluster that keeps its members together keeps its identifier however many documents join it. The first view treats a cluster as a group of documents, the second as a structure that recruits documents: which one fits depends on the question.

The rule needs documents present in successive windows. With successive windows (the default of build_dynamic_networks()), a network of documents shares no document from one window to the next (each document has a single year), and no cluster can be matched: sliding windows (window_step = 1) are necessary here.

window_networks <- networks # kept to compare other settings below
networks <- merge_dynamic_clusters(
  window_networks,
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id",
  threshold_similarity = 0.51,
  similarity_type = "partial"
)

How sensitive are the dynamic clusters to the threshold?

The threshold and the type of similarity decide how easily clusters are linked, hence how many dynamic clusters the history contains and how long they live. merge_diagnostics() runs the matching for a grid of thresholds and both similarity types, and plot_merge_diagnostics() draws the result.

diagnostics <- merge_diagnostics(
  window_networks,
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id",
  thresholds = c(0.51, 0.55, 0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.9),
  min_length = 3,
  verbose = FALSE
)
diagnostics[diagnostics$similarity_type == "partial",
            c("threshold", "n_dynamic_clusters", "share_continued", "median_lifespan",
              "n_persistent", "share_nodes_persistent")]
   threshold n_dynamic_clusters share_continued median_lifespan n_persistent

The 110 window clusters become 25 dynamic clusters at 0.51 and 89 at 0.9 with the complete similarity (19 and 54 with the partial one): the more demanding the threshold, the more clusters are considered new. The curves are flat between 0.51 and 0.55, so that values just above 0.5 are on a plateau: the continuities they produce do not depend on the exact threshold. They bend after 0.55, and the second view below shows what is lost. With the complete similarity, the median lifespan falls to one window at 0.75: every window then has its own clusters, which is the opposite of a history. The partial similarity is more tolerant, because it ignores the documents that enter or leave the corpus from one window to the next. This is the reason for the thresholds just above 0.5 with partial similarity in the studies that used networkflow: 0.501 for Delcey et al. (2026), 0.55 for Duluins et al. (2026). Whatever the choice, the continuities that a narrative relies on should survive close thresholds, and a different seed of the clustering.

plot_merge_diagnostics(diagnostics, view = "lifespans")

The second view shows who pays for a high threshold: the nodes of long clusters, which become members of short ones. With the complete similarity, the clusters that live more than ten windows gather about half of the nodes at 0.55 but 13% at 0.6, and none at 0.65: the longest continuities of the history are cut into shorter pieces between 0.55 and 0.65. With the partial similarity, such clusters still hold about 13% of the nodes at 0.9. The sensitivity of a continuity that matters for the story, here between 0.55 and 0.6, is exactly what the diagnostics are meant to reveal before it is hidden in a figure.

Other ways to follow clusters

The rule of merge_dynamic_clusters() is simple and transparent, with limits worth knowing. It compares a cluster only with the previous window, so a cluster that vanishes for one window and comes back gets a new identifier. Splits and merges are not recorded as such: the part that meets the double majority keeps the identifier, the others are new clusters. And the clusters of each window are detected independently, which adds instability between windows. Other approaches exist, and some could be tested on the same data:

Approach Idea Compared with the double majority
Overlap matching with a Jaccard threshold (Greene et al. 2010) Match the clusters of successive windows whose Jaccard similarity |Va∩Vb|/|Va∪Vb|\lvert V_a \cap V_b \rvert / \lvert V_a \cup V_b \rvert exceeds a threshold, and chain the matches into dynamic communities; splits and merges show up as one cluster matched to several. Symmetric by construction, and gives a name to events; a one-to-one assignment (best match first) could replace the majority rule.
Multislice community detection (Mucha et al. 2010) Detect communities in all windows at once, in a network where each node is tied to itself in adjacent windows with a coupling weight ω\omega. Identifiers are shared by construction. The coupling ω\omega plays the role of the threshold, but clusters of one window are influenced by the neighbouring windows: more stable, less independent. It needs nodes present in several windows (co-citation, authors, journals rather than documents).
Significance-clustered alluvial maps (Rosvall and Bergstrom 2010) Bootstrap the network to find which clusters are robust, then draw the flows between robust clusters. Addresses the instability of each partition rather than the matching rule; heavier.

Two simpler checks are available with the tools of the package: running the whole pipeline with several seeds of the clustering and comparing the dynamic clusters with merge_diagnostics(), and varying the window and its step (see the first guide), since instability often comes from windows that are too short to contain a stable structure. Implementing the first two approaches in the package, as alternatives to the double majority with the same output columns, would allow comparing them on real corpora.

Naming dynamic clusters

Once clusters are linked, each dynamic cluster can be named on all its documents across windows (name_merged_clusters = TRUE), with the words of the titles that distinguish it from the other dynamic clusters.

networks <- name_clusters(
  networks,
  method = "tf-idf",
  name_merged_clusters = TRUE,
  cluster_id = "dynamic_cluster_leiden",
  text_columns = "source_title",
  nb_terms_label = 3,
  clean_word_method = "lemmatize"
)

Drawing the history: alluvial plots

An alluvial plot shows the dynamic clusters as blocks in each window, with a height proportional to their share of the window, and flows that follow the documents from one window to the next. networks_to_alluv() stacks the node tables into the long table such a plot needs, with statistics on each cluster: its share of the whole history, its maximum share in a window, and the number of windows where it exists.

alluv_dt <- networks_to_alluv(
  networks,
  intertemporal_cluster_column = "dynamic_cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id"
)
cluster_stats <- unique(alluv_dt[, c("dynamic_cluster_leiden", "cluster_label",
                                     "share_cluster_max", "length_cluster")])
cluster_stats[order(-cluster_stats$length_cluster), ]

Clusters that exist in one or two windows, or remain small, clutter the plot. We keep the clusters that last at least three windows, give each a fixed colour, order the clusters to limit crossing flows (minimize_crossing = TRUE) and place each label in the middle of the cluster’s life (prepare_label = TRUE).

main_alluv <- alluv_dt[alluv_dt$length_cluster >= 3, ]
main_clusters <- sort(unique(main_alluv$dynamic_cluster_leiden))
palette <- data.frame(
  dynamic_cluster_leiden = main_clusters,
  color = scico::scico(length(main_clusters), palette = "batlow")
)
plot_alluvial(
  main_alluv,
  intertemporal_cluster_column = "dynamic_cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id",
  color_alluvial = TRUE,
  color = palette,
  minimize_crossing = TRUE,
  prepare_label = TRUE,
  cluster_label_column = "cluster_label"
) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of the window") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

The plot draws the history that Goutsmedt (2021) tells with qualitative and quantitative methods. The early windows are shared between clusters on wages, productivity, controls and unemployment, the explanations of the late 1970s and early 1980s, centred on supply shocks and inflation inertia. These clusters fade in the late 1980s, when windows contain few documents. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, clusters on disinflation and on time-consistent policy bridge the two periods. From the 1990s, new clusters appear, on the “great inflation” and policy rules, on peacetime inflation, and on oil prices and monetary alternatives, and last until the end of the period: a new literature, centred on monetary policy, in which the contributions of new classical economists, ignored by the first explanations, became major references (Goutsmedt 2021).

Reading the plot requires care. Flows between clusters are documents that change cluster when the window slides, which may reflect a change in the literature or simply the instability of a partition of a small network. Windows of a dozen documents give fragile clusters: their part of the plot should be read with the documents in hand.

Coordinates that follow the documents

To draw the networks of successive windows side by side, layout_networks(compute_dynamic_coordinates = TRUE) starts the layout of each window from the coordinates of the previous one, so that a document stays in the same region from one plot to the next. Giving the dynamic clusters the same colours as in the alluvial (color_networks() with the same palette) completes the picture: a cluster can be followed in the alluvial and located in each network.

set.seed(1)
networks <- layout_networks(
  networks,
  node_id = "source_id",
  layout = "fr",
  compute_dynamic_coordinates = TRUE
)
networks <- color_networks(networks, column_to_color = "dynamic_cluster_leiden", color = palette)

In research

The dynamic workflow was designed for histories of research fields, where the question is less “what are the communities?” than “when did a literature appear, what did it come from, and what did it become?”. Goutsmedt and Truc (2023) use bibliographic coupling and topic models to compare the macroeconomics published in the European Economic Review with the top five journals, between 1969 and 2002. Delcey et al. (2026) follow the discussions of rationality in a corpus of nearly 260,000 economics articles from 1900 to 2009. Duluins et al. (2026) apply the same tools to the scientific reception of a report on the environmental impact of livestock. In each case, the networks do not replace reading: they tell the historian which documents to read, and which continuities and breaks need an explanation.

References
